## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**Whole chapter**
- Ellicott sees the main point as God's punishment arriving slowly but surely. It falls on Gideon's house for his two late failings: taking many wives, and dabbling in worship God hadn't authorised and that came close to idolatry. (Ellicott)
- Enduring Word calls Abimelech Israel's first self-proclaimed king: a godless leader given to a godless people, which leads only to ruin. (EW)
- Matthew Henry notes that the people of Shechem were punished by the very man they had wrongly raised up. (MHC)

**v. 1**
- Throughout the chapter Gideon is called "Jerubbaal," and the Pulpit Commentary thinks there must be a reason for this. (Pulpit)
- Ellicott thinks Abimelech moved soon after Gideon died and had probably been planning for a long time. (Ellicott)
- Gill thinks Abimelech grew up in his father's house at Ophrah and came to Shechem to visit his uncles. (Gill-SL)
- JFB says the idolatry that had crept in during Gideon's last years was now practised openly, and idol-worshippers held the upper hand in Shechem. (JFB)
- JFB also sees here a clear example of the harm done by having many wives: one son ends up with family ties and interests quite apart from his brothers'. (BH 9:1)
- One commentary on the Bible Hub page suggests his mother may have fed his ambition. It also suggests his name, which carries the idea of royalty, may have encouraged him. (BH 9:1)
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says a son can be badly raised away from a godly father's eye. It calls the whole episode a clear judgment on Gideon's sin of marrying a Canaanite. (PHC)

**v. 2**
- Gill: judges' sons never inherited their fathers' rule, and nothing suggests any of Gideon's sons wanted to rule. The "seventy rulers" idea was a wicked hint planted by Abimelech. (Gill)
- Keil & Delitzsch: no such rule by the seventy ever existed. Abimelech assumed his brothers were as hungry for power as he was. To Baal-worshipping Shechem, even the name "sons of Jerubbaal" (the man who tore down Baal's altar) would not have helped them. (BH 9:1)
- Constable makes the same point: nothing in the text shows the brothers wanted to be king. (Constable)
- Ellicott says "men of Shechem" should be "lords (*baali*) of Shechem." He thinks Canaanites may still have held the fortress there. (Ellicott-SL)
- "Your flesh and blood" means a kinsman from the same tribe and city. (Gill; BH 9:1)

**v. 3**
- "He is our brother" meant his rise would be good for them. (BH 9:1)
- Shechem was where Joshua had held his last great assembly. Winning that city would be a big step for Abimelech. (BH 9:1)

**v. 4**
- Enduring Word cites Adam Clarke: a work begun in the devil's name, here paid for from Baal-berith's temple, is unlikely to end to God's glory. (EW)
- JFB: "Baal-berith" means "god of the covenant," the god invoked when the league of cities was formed. (JFB)
- JFB describes the hired men as worthless drifters with nothing to lose and much to gain from a revolt. (JFB)

**v. 5**
- Ellicott suggests that, like Absalom, Abimelech may have struck at a family feast when all his brothers were gathered. (Ellicott)
- JFB says "on one stone" could mean throwing them from one rock. Or it could mean sacrificing them on one stone altar, as revenge for their father destroying Baal's altar. (JFB)
- Constable takes "on one stone" as a sign of a well-planned mass murder. (Constable)
- Enduring Word: the men of Shechem backed the plan because it was good *for them*, not because it was right. (EW)
- Enduring Word also links the stone to his death later in the chapter. It quotes Trapp: he killed his brothers on one stone, and a stone kills him. (EW)

**v. 6**
- Enduring Word: it's hard to say who was worse, the murderer or the men who approved of him. Quoting Wolf, Abimelech was the first man crowned king in Israel, yet he ignored God's requirements for that office. (EW)
- Ellicott: he was the first Israelite to hold the title "king," probably only within Ephraim. Gideon had refused both "king" and "ruler." (Ellicott-SL)
- Ellicott says it's unclear whether "Beth-millo" is a place name or means the people of Millo. (Ellicott)
- JFB takes "the house of Millo" as the people in the temple, that is, Baal's priests. It renders the setting "by the oak near a raised mound," so the crowd could see the crowning. (JFB)

**v. 7**
- Keil & Delitzsch say Jotham's opening appeal recalls the language of the prophets. They call his story the earliest fable we know of, with real prophetic meaning. (BH 9:15)

**v. 8**
- Ellicott: this passing mention shows that neighbouring nations also anointed their kings. The olive tree would naturally come to mind first because it was so valuable and fruitful. (Ellicott)

**v. 9**
- Ellicott: the Hebrew could also mean "which gods and men honour in me." Either way, "God" refers to oil used in sacrifices, offerings and consecrations. (Ellicott)
- The Pulpit Commentary agrees. Oil honours God in the grain offerings and honours people when kings, priests and prophets are anointed. (BH 9:9)
- Gill and Benson note that "be promoted" literally means to sway or wander to and fro. It pictures giving up a settled, useful life for the endless worries of ruling. (Gill-SL; BH 9:9)
- Gill draws a lesson from this. A good person need not leave a private calling where they serve usefully to take on a burdensome public office. (Gill-SL)

**vv. 10–13**
- Matthew Henry's comments on this passage note that all three fruit trees give much the same reason for refusing. Ruling brings heavy work and worry. (BH 9:9)
- They also say those who bear fruit for the common good deserve more honour than those who merely cut a figure. (BH 9:9)
- Keil & Delitzsch sum up the trees' answer: should we give up bearing valuable fruit for God and people just to rise above the other trees? (BH 9:9)
- The Layman's Bible Commentary says the noble trees refusing stands for Gideon turning down the kingship. (LBC)

**v. 14**
- Ellicott notes that the trees speak to the thornbush with a blunter command than they used for the olive, fig and vine. (Ellicott)
- The bramble stands for Abimelech. (LBC; MHC; Constable)

**v. 15**
- Ellicott calls the speech biting irony. A bramble gives almost no shade, and what it gives is dangerous. Its threats probably echo threats Abimelech had made. (BH 9:15)
- Gill: anyone who shelters under a bramble just gets scratched. (BH 9:15)
- Gill also says the "cedars" are the leading men, who would suffer if they weren't loyal to him. (Gill)
- Constable: brambles can burst into flame in hot weather. On his reading the cedars are Shechem's upright leaders. (Constable)
- The Pulpit Commentary: "in truth" means with sincere intent. The bramble's speech already hints at mistrust between Abimelech and Shechem. (BH 9:15)

**vv. 16–18**
- Ellicott: here Jotham applies the fable. Verses 16–18 are a long chain of "if" clauses, and the conclusion comes in v. 19. (Ellicott)
- The Cambridge Bible, on the Bible Hub page, thinks the fable is dropped here. What follows is a rebuke for ingratitude and a warning, not a strict application. (BH 9:15)
- The Pulpit Commentary: putting Gideon's great deeds next to their bloody act made a charge they couldn't answer. (Pulpit)
- Ellicott: "son of his maidservant" is meant as an insult. Judges 8:31 and 9:1 suggest she was not a slave and may even have been a high-born Canaanite. (Ellicott)
- Enduring Word: the real reason Shechem backed Abimelech was that he was their "brother" through his mother. (EW)

**v. 19**
- Gill: Jotham offers a test. If the alliance turned out happy, that would prove they had acted rightly, but Jotham himself didn't believe it would. (Gill)
- The Pulpit Commentary calls his good wishes "lofty scorn and irony." (Pulpit)

**v. 20**
- Ellicott: the curse is that the two sides destroy each other. It was exactly fulfilled in vv. 45–49. (Ellicott)
- The Pulpit Commentary says the same: an alliance built on bloodshed ends in mutual hatred. It notes the fire at the tower (v. 49) literally fulfilled vv. 15 and 20. (Pulpit)
- Enduring Word also links the curse to the massacre at the tower. (EW)

**v. 21**
- Ellicott: "Beer" means "well," so it was a very common place name. (Ellicott)

**v. 22**
- Ellicott: the verb for "reigned" here differs from the one in v. 6, but we can't tell whether that matters. "Over Israel" means whoever would accept him, mainly the central tribes. (Ellicott)
- JFB: the word means "despotism," as opposed to a judge's mild, God-given rule. JFB thinks his rule spread slowly out from Shechem. (JFB)
- Enduring Word cites Wolf: the word appears only in this book and marks Abimelech as more tyrant than king. (EW)
- Gill: it's amazing that Israel didn't rise up to avenge Gideon's sons. Abimelech's rule was short, as wicked rulers' often are. (Gill)

**vv. 23–24**
- The Pulpit Commentary: these two verses summarise the rest of the chapter. Everything that follows happened by God's providence so that the brothers' blood would come back on Abimelech and Shechem. (Pulpit)
- Enduring Word: after three calm years, God took away the peace between them as a judgment. Power won by violence turns on itself. (EW)
- For the different views on what the "spirit" was, see section 2.

**v. 25**
- Constable thinks the men of Shechem were robbing Abimelech of the tolls he collected from travellers and traders. (Constable)

**v. 26**
- The Pulpit Commentary says nobody knows who Gaal was. He looks like an opportunist using the growing discontent for his own ends. Some manuscripts read "Eber" instead of "Ebed." (Pulpit)
- Gill also says his origins are uncertain. (Gill)

**v. 27**
- Ellicott: grape harvest was the most joyful festival of the year. The word for "festival" appears elsewhere only in Leviticus 19:24, where it means "praise." He sees this as a pagan copy of Israel's Feast of Ingathering. (Ellicott; Ellicott-SL)
- The Pulpit Commentary, quoted by Precept Austin: they held the festival in Baal-berith's temple and, loosened by wine, cursed Abimelech. (PA)
- Enduring Word: these were drunken parties, confident in their new leader. (EW)

**v. 28**
- Gill paraphrases Gaal's taunt: Abimelech has no better right to rule than the descendants of old Shechem, who actually have the better claim. (Gill-SL)
- Gill on "son of Jerubbaal": his father tore down the altar of the very Baal you now serve. (Gill-SL)
- Gill on "Zebul his officer": Abimelech has even set a deputy over you, which means harsh rule. (Gill-SL)

## 2. Where readings differ

I found no clear Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal, Reformed, Lutheran or Anglican disagreement, because I couldn't reach those sites.

The one real split in the sources I did read is **v. 23, "God sent a spirit"**:
- **JFB:** in the normal course of providence, jealousy and rebellion arose, and God *permitted* them as punishment. (JFB)
- **Gill:** God permitted, and even commissioned, Satan to stir up suspicion. Or God handed them over to their own desires. (Gill-SL)
- **Ellicott:** we can't say whether the "spirit" is a personal being or just a bad temper. The Hebrew word is used both ways. (Ellicott)
- **Constable:** a spirit of discontent. (Constable)
- **Layman's Bible Commentary:** a Hebrew way of describing a demonic element entering a situation. It also asks whether saying God "permits" it is just a softer way of repeating what the author meant. (LBC)

---

## 3. Other views

I found nothing from bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org, the Catholic and Orthodox sites, or about prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching. Two related points from the pages I did read:
- The Layman's Bible Commentary takes a more historical angle. It says the story shows Canaanites still held big cities like Shechem, and that Canaanites and Israelites were merging. (LBC)
- Constable cites G. Ernest Wright's archaeological study of Shechem. (Constable)

To fill these gaps, the next pages to read would be: the netbible.org notes on Judges 9; the Haydock (Catholic) commentary listed on Bible Hub's verse pages; gotquestions.org on Jotham's parable and on "evil spirit from God"; and samstorms.org or desiringgod.org on God's sovereignty and evil spirits.
